name: overhead-from-the-top
prompt: Tall portrait frame. We are perched on the summit of a colossal pile of printed paperwork, peering vertically down its flank: a pale cliff of stacked page edges, tens of metres high, narrowing in steep perspective toward a rain-slicked concrete warehouse floor at the bottom. Closest to the lens, lying flat and razor sharp, the uppermost page carries two words set in fat black sans-serif capitals: THE RULES. Far beneath, tiny and a touch out of focus, a crew of five stand in a loose huddle, heads tipped right back so their masked faces stare up into the lens. They are dressed like any group on a British street today: tracksuit tops, a waterproof parka, a padded gilet, trainers and work boots, gloves on both hands, cuffs pulled down to meet the gloves, collars zipped to the chin. Every head is wrapped in a seamless cloth hood with a blank surface where the features would be, each hood a different deep shade: midnight blue, forest green, slate, wine, soot black. On each, a bold white circle is sewn as a band that frames the face, and one red triangle sits high near its edge over the wearer's left eye, so from our viewpoint it lands at roughly two o'clock, up and to the right, clearly off-centre. Fabric only, nothing mechanical or shiny. The crew aim pocket flashlights upwards; those beams are the only real light, slicing through drifting dust and splashing bright ovals up the paper face, catching the sewn circles and triangles so they gleam. A thin amber streetlamp glow seeps through a small high window and grazes one side of the stack. Everything else is near-total darkness, wet floor reflections and hard white spots. Ultra-wide lens, vertiginous drop, inky shadows, coarse grain.
